name: ONS — Effects of taxes and benefits on household income (tax-benefits-statistics, time-series v3)
published: 2022-09-09 (dct:issued of dataset version 3; the bulletin series runs later — see raw/README.md on why the version is pinned rather than following latest_version)

model.name: ONS Effects of Taxes and Benefits household income model
model.method: Household survey microdata (Household Finances Survey / Living Costs and Food Survey) with direct taxes and cash benefits attributed per household, indirect taxes imputed from expenditure, and benefits in kind (health, education, housing subsidy, rail/bus travel subsidy, school meals) allocated by usage and population share. Households are ranked into quintile groups by EQUIVALISED DISPOSABLE income.
model.method_basis: ONS Effects of Taxes and Benefits Quality and Methodology Information

income_concepts.original: market income before any state intervention

income_concept_note: Five running totals of the same household, one per stage of the tax-benefit system — five quantities, not one with a qualifier. Summing or comparing across them is a category error, and every row carries which stage it is.
ranking_note: The dataset labels its dimension only 'Quintile'. That the ranking is by EQUIVALISED DISPOSABLE income on the modified-OECD scale comes from the ETB Quality and Methodology Information, which is stable across editions — so the axis name records the methodology and this note cites where it comes from, rather than the dataset asserting it. The quintiles are recorded DISTINCT from UKMOD's, IFS's and Resolution Foundation's groupings, exhaustively. They are NOT recorded distinct from HBAI's, deliberately: HBAI registers no decile or quantile vocabulary, so there is nothing on that side to assert against. period: Mixed by design: calendar years 1977-1993 and financial years 1994-95 to 2020-21. ONS's own code list is named `financial-and-calendar-years`. Each row carries the time basis its label implies, and a financial year keys its END year.
geographies: United Kingdom (the dataset's only geography value)
coverage_note: Source reconciliation: 5,280 published observations = 2,640 claims + 2,640 deliberate drops. The dropped half is the `Deflated value` series, whose PRICE BASE is stated nowhere in the dataset, its CSVW metadata, or the `value-deflation` code list; a real-terms figure with an unknown base year cannot be reproduced or compared. The 2024 bulletin names CPIH excluding Council Tax, but that is a different release from this version-3 dataset and attributing its deflator here would launder one publication's methodology onto another's numbers. Quintiles, not deciles: the decile table on the legacy dataset page is a 2015-saved .xls from a discontinued series (raw/README.md).
not_expressible_note: Corrected after reading the certified engine rather than assuming. BENEFITS IN KIND are NOT a total coverage gap: PolicyEngine-UK models four of ONS's five components — health (gov/dhsc nhs_spending, itself A&E + outpatient + admitted patient), education (gov/dfe dfe_education_spending), school meals (gov/dfe free_school_meals) and travel subsidies (gov/dft rail_subsidy_spending, bus_subsidy_spending). Only the HOUSING SUBSIDY component has no counterpart. So `final` income is PARTIAL, not not_expressible, and every final-income claim carries pe_missing naming the one component that is short. Calling it a total gap would have let a real divergence on the four modelled components be waved away as 'PolicyEngine doesn't do this' — the opposite failure to the one the gate exists for. Indirect taxes are likewise partial: PE-UK has vat and the individual duties but no single indirect-tax aggregate, so a post-tax counterpart must sum the heads.
diagnosis_upstream: Divergences decompose against the survey base (ONS uses HFS/LCFS; PE-UK's certified world is FRS-based), the equivalisation scale, the indirect-tax imputation, and the benefits-in-kind allocation, before any engine defect is named — and then only through the citable-known-issue gate.
